title: Observability for designers
summary: Observability is what lets a team ask a new question of a running system without shipping new code to answer it. This lesson gives the four golden signals and the symptoms-against-causes rule as tables, explains what traces, metrics and logs each record and how a trace id joins them, states what each kind of component must emit, sets a cardinality budget for metric labels, describes one structured log entry per unit of work, head and tail sampling of traces, and the collector pipeline, then sizes the telemetry of one service from its request rate.

blocks.text: Google's SRE book states the cost of doing this well: even with shared infrastructure for collection, display and alerting, an SRE team of 10 to 12 people typically has one or two members whose primary job is the service's monitoring. Its Bigtable case shows the alternative. The service's SLO was based on a synthetic client's mean performance, which a slow tail dominated, so email and paging alerts fired voluminously and the team missed the problems that affected users. The remedy was to dial the SLO back temporarily to the 75th percentile latency and disable the email alerts, which bought the time to fix the storage stack underneath.

Amazon's service teams log one structured entry per unit of work and derive their metrics from the log afterwards. The guidance gives DynamoDB as the limit case: serving over 20 million requests per second of internal traffic at peak, it still logs every request, for troubleshooting and for audit. The same article describes how the teams make that affordable, including rotating log files every minute and running load tests for hours to prove that the log-shipping agents keep up at maximum throughput.

blocks.text: OpenTelemetry's gateway documentation describes a topology for tail sampling: a first collector tier whose load-balancing exporter routes by trace id to a second tier running the tail sampling processor, so that spans of a trace reach the collector that makes the decision. This is project deployment guidance, not evidence of adoption.

subtopics.title: What observability is for: symptoms, causes and the golden signals

blocks.text: The OpenTelemetry primer defines observability as the ability to understand a system from the outside by asking questions about it without knowing its inner workings, including questions nobody thought to ask before the incident. The test it proposes is practical: an application is properly instrumented when developers do not need to add more instrumentation to troubleshoot an issue. Google's SRE book uses the older word, monitoring, for the collection, processing, aggregation and display of real-time quantitative data, and separates white-box monitoring, which reads the internals of the system through its own instrumentation, from black-box monitoring, which tests externally visible behaviour as a user would see it.

The same chapter gives the distinction that organises everything else: a monitoring system answers two questions, what is broken and why. The first is a symptom and the second a cause, and the chapter's examples show that a cause is often several layers below the symptom a user sees.

blocks.caption: Symptoms and causes from the SRE book's own table.
rows: CPUs overloaded by a bad sort, or a crimped cable showing as partial packet loss
Users in one region are not receiving content
the CDN blocklisted some client IPs
a software push caused ACLs to be forgotten

blocks.text: For a user-facing system the chapter names four signals that must be measured whatever else is: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. It adds two refinements that instrumentation often gets wrong. The latency of failed requests must be tracked separately from the latency of successful ones, because a fast error is still a failure and a slow error is worse. And errors include implicit failures, such as a success status with the wrong content, and policy failures, such as any request slower than a committed bound.

blocks.caption: The four golden signals.
rows: keep success and error latency apart; p99 over a short window is an early sign of saturation
requests per second for a web service; sessions or I/O rate for streaming; transactions per second for a store
explicit (500s), implicit (wrong content with a 200), by policy (slower than the bound)
measure the most constrained resource; many systems degrade before 100 percent, so set a utilisation target

blocks.text: Measure the four golden signals for every user-facing service. Page on urgent, actionable user impact or imminent failure; cause-level signals usually belong on diagnostic dashboards, but may justify paging when they establish such a threat.

subtopics.title: Traces, metrics and logs, and how a trace id joins them

blocks.text: The OpenTelemetry primer describes three signals. A metric is an aggregation over a period of numeric data about infrastructure or an application, such as an error rate or a request rate. A log is a timestamped message that is not necessarily associated with any particular request. A span represents a single unit of work with a name, timing data, structured messages and attributes, and a trace is the tree of spans for one request, starting at a root span. The primer's own observation is that logs are far more useful once they are correlated with a trace and a span.

blocks.caption: What each signal records and what it is good for.
rows: a number per label set per scrape interval
the number of label combinations, not the request rate
is something wrong, and since when
a tree of spans for one request, each with a start, a duration and attributes
the request rate times spans per request, so it is sampled
where in the call tree the time or the error is
a structured entry for one unit of work, or a free-form line
the request rate times bytes per entry

blocks.text: The join between the signals is an identifier. Amazon's engineering guidance describes a trace id as a meta request id stamped on a distributed unit of work by the front-door service and propagated to every dependency, so that the log entries of many services can be lined up for one request. OpenTelemetry SDKs can correlate logs with traces by injecting the trace id and span id into log records when the logging integration and active context are configured. This lets a reader move from a slow span to the log lines written inside it.

Two consequences follow for a design. First, every service in a request path must forward the context, because one hop that drops it splits the trace into unrelated pieces; Amazon's teams found framework-level propagation unreliable in multi-threaded code and pass the trace id and a metrics object explicitly in method signatures. Second, the attributes that name a service, its version and its environment must be spelled the same way on all three signals, or a dashboard panel, a trace search and a log query cannot be filtered to the same set of instances.
Decide the naming of services, versions, environments and routes once, in a shared library or collector configuration, before fifty services each invent their own.

subtopics.title: What each kind of component must emit

blocks.text: The Prometheus instrumentation guidance sorts services into three types and names the metrics that matter for each. An online-serving system, where a human or another system waits for the reply, needs its query count, errors and latency, and ideally the count of requests in progress; it should be measured on both the client and the server side, because a disagreement between the two sides is itself diagnostic. Offline processing, where nobody is waiting, needs per stage the items in, in progress and out, and the last time the stage processed anything. A batch job needs the time it last succeeded, pushed rather than scraped because the job is not running when the scraper calls.

blocks.caption: The three types of system and what each must expose.
rows: query count, errors, latency, in-progress requests
count queries when they end, so counts line up with latency and errors
per stage: items in, in progress, out; last processed time
a heartbeat item's timestamp stops advancing
send a dummy item through the pipeline to measure propagation time
last success time, stage durations, total runtime
push to a gateway; for a job running more often than every 15 minutes, consider conversion to a daemon

blocks.text: Two mnemonics cover the request path and the machines under it. RED, from Tom Wilkie, records for every service the request rate, the error count and the duration distribution, so that every service looks the same and people can be on call for code they did not write. USE, from Brendan Gregg, records for every resource its utilisation, saturation and errors. The Grafana write-up calls them two views of one system, users and machines, and notes that the golden signals are RED plus saturation.

Below the service level, the Prometheus guidance wants metrics from every library that touches an outside resource, every thread pool and every cache. Amazon's list comes from operating services and is the one to copy into a design review.

items: The availability and latency of every dependency, per call, per resource and per status code, so a retry storm or a throttled table is visible as such.
The depth of every queue the request touches, and the time each item waited in it, which needs an enqueue timestamp on the message.
A counter per error reason, grouped at least into the client's fault and the server's fault.
A separate latency timer for successful responses, so that fast errors do not make latency look good.
Enough metadata to know who called and what for, allowing fields into logs only through an opt-in policy that excludes sensitive data.

blocks.text: A design review names, per component, the type it belongs to and the metrics above. A component for which that list cannot be written is not ready to ship.

subtopics.title: Metric types, labels and the cardinality budget

blocks.text: The Prometheus guidance gives one rule for the first choice: if the value can go down, it is a gauge; otherwise it is a counter, queried through a rate because a raw counter is rarely useful. For distributions there are two approaches, and the histograms document is explicit about the difference. A summary has the instrumented program compute fixed quantiles over a fixed window, which is accurate but cannot be recomputed for another window and, most importantly, cannot be aggregated across replicas. A histogram counts observations into buckets, which can be summed across instances and queried for any quantile later; the document's advice is to use native histograms where the library and server support them and classic histograms otherwise.

blocks.caption: The four metric types and what each is for.
rows: only goes up, resets on restart
in-progress requests, queue depth, free memory, a last-success timestamp
the current value; never rate() it
counts per bucket plus a sum and a count
latency and sizes that must be aggregated across replicas
histogram_quantile() after summing buckets; each classic bucket is its own series
a single instance where the quantile cannot be recomputed later

blocks.text: Labels are what make one metric answer many questions: one http_responses_total with a code label rather than a metric per status code, so a rule or a graph can treat the whole as one. The cost is that every distinct label set is a separate time series with its own memory, CPU, disk and network, and the guidance is to keep the cardinality of a metric below ten, to limit the few that exceed it to a handful across the whole system, and to treat a metric with over a hundred label values, or the potential to grow that large, as a sign that the analysis belongs in a general processing system rather than in monitoring.

blocks.title: The cardinality arithmetic from the Prometheus guidance
items: A node exporter exposes a filesystem metric for every mounted filesystem, in the tens of series per node.
Across 10,000 nodes that is roughly 100,000 series for that one metric, which the guidance calls fine for Prometheus to handle.
Add a per-user quota label with 10,000 users on the same nodes and the count becomes a double-digit number of millions of series.
The guidance calls that too much for the current implementation, and notes the opportunity cost: those series displace other, more useful metrics on the same server.

blocks.text: User ids, request ids and raw URL paths are unbounded label values. Route templates and status classes are bounded. Send the unbounded detail to traces or logs, where one record costs one record rather than one series for ever.

subtopics.title: Logs: one structured entry per unit of work

blocks.text: Amazon's instrumentation guidance describes two kinds of log. The request log holds one structured entry per unit of work, a request received or a message pulled from a queue, carrying properties about the request and its caller, counters of how often things happened and timers of how long they took; it serves as an audit log and as a trace of everything that happened in the service. The application log holds unstructured debug lines. The structured log is the source of the metrics: Amazon's services log first and compute aggregates afterwards, so one approach yields both the dashboards and the per-request detail.

blocks.caption: Amazon's request log practices and the reason for each.
rows: Emit exactly one entry per unit of work, serialised after all stages complete
one place to look for a failed request; several entries per request multiply the cost
Record the request's details before validation or throttling can reject it, sanitised and truncated
a rejected request is the one you need to see; a caller must not be able to inject into the log
Log the availability and latency of every dependency, per call and per resource
otherwise explaining a slow request means comparing graphs and guessing
Emit a 1 for success and a 0 for failure
the mean is availability only when both successes and failures are recorded
Keep a separate timer for successful responses
fast errors and throttling otherwise make latency look better than it is
Log a trace id and pass it to every dependency
lines from many services can be lined up for one request
Opt in to logging approved fields, excluding sensitive data; protect the log with access control and encryption
a sensitive parameter added later is not logged by default

blocks.text: The guidance is candid that this is expensive and worth it, and gives the measures that make it affordable at high throughput: sample entries with each kept entry recording how many were skipped; move serialisation and flushing to a separate thread; rotate files every minute so the shipping agent reads from the page cache; and load test for hours to prove the shipper keeps up, because a disk that fills with logs takes the service down.

The Prometheus guidance adds the link back to metrics: for every line of logging code there should be a counter, so that an interesting message can be asked how often it has been happening and for how long.

An application log that grows into the request path, with a line per stage and a stack trace per error, can impose substantial cost. Rate-limit error spam, keep debug levels off in production, and put the per-request facts in the one structured entry.

Google's Dapper paper set the model that OpenTelemetry follows. A trace is a tree of spans; each span has a name, a span id and a parent id, a span without a parent is a root span, and every span of one request carries the same trace id. Instrumentation lives in the shared RPC and threading libraries, so most applications are traced without changes, and collection is out of band, so the traced request never waits on the tracing system.

Propagation is the part a designer must get right at every boundary. The context carries the trace id and the span id; when service A calls service B, B creates a span in the same trace with A's span as its parent. A propagator serialises the context into the call, by default as the W3C traceparent header: a version, the trace id, the parent span id and trace flags. Libraries do this for HTTP and RPC; a design must make the same happen through message headers on a queue and across thread pools, because any hop that drops the context ends the trace. The page also warns against trusting context from outside callers, who can forge headers.

OpenTelemetry's guidance is to sample once a system produces about a thousand traces a second and most describe healthy traffic, and not at tens of traces a second or where regulation forbids dropping data. The two mechanisms differ in what they know when they decide.

blocks.caption: Head sampling against tail sampling.
rows: at the start, from the trace id and a target percentage
after the trace completes, from its spans
consistent trace-id selection with complete propagation
configured error or latency policies can retain matching traces if upstream delivery, buffering and capacity are sufficient
cheap; runs anywhere in the pipeline
a stateful tier that buffers spans and must itself be monitored
cannot keep all errors; the outcome is unknown at the start
every span of a trace must reach the same node, which shapes the topology

blocks.caption: Dapper's measured cost of tracing a web search cluster.

blocks.text: Dapper's first production version sampled one trace in 1,024 uniformly, enough for high-throughput services because a pattern that occurs once will occur thousands of times, while a service handling dozens of requests a second can trace all of them. Hence adaptive sampling: a target number of sampled traces per unit time rather than a fixed probability, with the probability used recorded on each trace so that analyses can weight it.

Propagate context through every boundary. Choose sampling from trace volume; tail policies can prioritize errors only when their spans reach the deciding collector. Monitor drops and buffering, and record sampling probability.

subtopics.title: The telemetry pipeline: collectors, agents and gateways

blocks.text: Between the instrumented services and the stores sits a pipeline, and OpenTelemetry's Collector is the common shape of it. Its configuration names receivers, which accept data in a protocol such as OTLP; processors, which change or drop data as it passes; exporters, which send it on; and connectors, which join pipelines. The processors are where policy lives: the documented examples insert an environment attribute, delete a db.statement attribute, hash an email attribute, filter spans and log records by expression, sample traces by probability, and the memory limiter refuses data once the process nears its limit so that the pipeline sheds load instead of dying.

blocks.legend: Services export OTLP to a collector next to them; the agents forward to a gateway pool per cluster or region, which samples traces and fans out to one store per signal (s7).

blocks.text: The gateway pattern is a single OTLP endpoint per cluster, data centre or region, served by a pool of collectors behind an ordinary load balancer, with applications or other collectors sending to it. Its documented benefits are centrally managed credentials and one place for policy such as filtering and sampling; its documented costs are one more thing to maintain and that can fail, added latency when collectors are cascaded, and more total resources. Where a decision needs every span of a trace, the pattern becomes two tiers: the first tier runs a load-balancing exporter that routes by trace id, so that all spans of a trace reach the same second-tier collector, where the tail sampling policy is applied.

blocks.caption: Where each stage of the pipeline runs and what it is for.
rows: next to the workload, as a sidecar or one per node
receives over the local network, adds host and orchestrator attributes, batches and retries
memory on every node; configuration pushed everywhere
a pool per cluster or region behind a load balancer
credentials, filtering, redaction, sampling, fan-out to stores
a service to run and monitor; cascade latency
a pool fed by the load-balancing exporter
tail sampling with trace-id routing; span-based metrics may instead require service-based routing and distinct writer identities
stateful buffering; the single-writer rule for metrics

blocks.text: One rule from the gateway documentation catches a subtle fault: every metric stream must have a single writer with a globally unique identity. Two collectors reporting the same series produce gaps, jumps and out-of-order samples in the store, and the page shows the error a Prometheus backend prints when that happens.

The pipeline is a data path with the same failure modes as the system it observes. Give it memory limits, back-pressure and its own golden signals, or it will fall over during the incident it exists to explain.

subtopics.title: Alerts and dashboards that follow from the design

blocks.text: The SRE chapter's rule for paging is to alert on symptoms, and to reserve cause-oriented rules for dashboards and for the few causes that are very definite and very imminent, such as a disk that will fill in four hours. Its reasoning is cost: a page interrupts someone's work or sleep, and when pages come too often people skim or ignore them, including the real one. The chapter offers five questions to ask of any proposed rule.

items: Does this rule detect an otherwise undetected condition that is urgent, actionable, and actively or imminently user-visible?
Will I ever be able to ignore this alert knowing it is benign, and if so, how do I filter that case out?
Does this alert definitely indicate that users are being negatively affected? Are there cases, such as drained traffic or test deployments, that should be excluded?
Can I act on it, is the action urgent, could it be automated, and is it a fix or a workaround?
Is someone else already being paged for the same issue?

blocks.text: From those questions the chapter draws a philosophy: every page should be actionable, should require intelligence rather than a rote response, and should be about a novel problem. It also sets expectations for resolution and simplicity. For a service targeting about nine hours of downtime a year, probing for success more than once or twice a minute is unnecessary; rules that catch real incidents should be as simple and predictable as possible; and a signal that no dashboard shows and no alert uses is a candidate for removal.

The design deliverable is therefore a short table per component, written before launch and read during incidents: what proves the component healthy, what pages, and the first query an on-call engineer runs. The burn-rate alerts that page on an objective belong in the reliability lesson; what matters here is that every row rests on a signal the component actually emits.

blocks.caption: A telemetry sheet for one design, one row per component.
rows: success rate and p99 latency per route
the error or latency objective is at risk
errors by route and reason, last 15 minutes
items in, out and in progress; oldest item age
oldest item age exceeds the freshness bound
queue depth and dependency latency per call
latency as clients see it and as it sees itself
saturation threatens imminent user-visible failure and requires action
slow statements with their trace ids
received, dropped and exported counts; memory
sustained drops threaten required visibility and require urgent action

blocks.text: Page on urgent user-visible symptoms or actionable imminent failure. Use causes primarily for diagnosis. Keep paging rules simple and remove unused signals.

worked_example.title: Worked example: sizing the telemetry of an order service at 2,000 requests per second

blocks.text: An order service wants its metrics, logs and traces designed before launch. Inputs below are assumptions, with peak load sustained throughout each day and decimal byte units. The Python sample illustrates instrumentation, not recomputation or an exact implementation of the series estimate; the tables give the sizing arithmetic.

blocks.title: From request rate to telemetry volume
items: Peak load: 2,000 requests per second across the service (assumption), served by 30 instances (assumption).
Routes: the API has 20 route templates (assumption); status is labelled by class, 5 values, never by raw path or customer id.
Request counter: 20 routes times 5 status classes is 100 series per instance.
Latency histogram: assume 12 buckets including infinity, plus sum and count, giving 14 series per route and 280 per instance; omit client-created and runtime series from this estimate.
Per instance that is 380 series; across 30 instances, 11,400 series for the service, well inside what the Prometheus guidance calls fine.
The tempting mistake: a customer label with 50,000 customers (assumption) would multiply the 11,400 by 50,000, into the hundreds of millions of series, which the guidance refuses.
Logs: one structured entry per request at 1 kB (assumption) is 2 MB per second, or about 173 GB per day.
Log retention of 30 days (assumption) is about 5.2 TB before compression, so the entry size and the retention are the two numbers to negotiate.
Traces: 6 spans per request at 400 bytes each (assumption) is 2.4 kB per trace; tracing everything would be 4.8 MB per second, about 415 GB per day.
At 2,000 traces per second the volume is above OpenTelemetry's threshold of about 1,000 per second, so sampling applies.
Disable upstream head sampling: all spans reach a trace-affine tail collector. Select errors OR a 5 percent probabilistic sample there.
Assume 0.5 percent of traces carry ERROR status and complete delivery: errors contribute 2.0736 GB/day; sampling only the remaining healthy volume contributes 20.63232 GB/day.
The union is 22.70592 GB/day, not the sum of a sample of all traces plus errors. Logs at 172.8 GB/day dominate stored traces; the tail tier still receives 414.72 GB/day before sampling.

blocks.caption: The telemetry estimate as a reviewer should receive it.
rows: 20 routes times 5 classes, plus 20 times 14 histogram series
healthy sample plus errors; no overlap

blocks.code:
import logging, time
from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, start_http_server
from opentelemetry import trace

# bounded labels only: a route template and a status class, never a user id or a raw path
REQS = Counter("http_requests_total", "Requests", ["route", "code_class"])
LAT = Histogram("http_request_duration_seconds", "Latency of successful requests", ["route"])
log = logging.getLogger("request")

def handle(route, work):
    span = trace.get_current_span().get_span_context()   # set by the server instrumentation
    start = time.perf_counter()
    code_class, error_reason = "2xx", None
    try:
        return work()
    except Exception as e:
        code_class, error_reason = "5xx", type(e).__name__
        raise
    finally:
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        REQS.labels(route, code_class).inc()
        if code_class == "2xx":
            LAT.labels(route).observe(elapsed)            # a separate timer for successes
        log.info("request", extra={                     # one structured entry per unit of work
            "route": route, "code_class": code_class, "error_reason": error_reason,
            "duration_ms": round(elapsed * 1000, 1),
            "trace_id": format(span.trace_id, "032x"), "span_id": format(span.span_id, "016x"),
        })

start_http_server(8000)   # exposes /metrics for scraping
blocks.caption: Illustrative instrumentation only. Default client buckets and extra created/runtime series differ from the estimate. Configure an INFO-level structured logging handler to serialize the extra fields; this fragment does not configure that handler or the server's tracing SDK.

blocks.code:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 5s
    limit_mib: 4000
    spike_limit_mib: 500
  attributes:
    actions:
      - key: db.statement
        action: delete
      - key: email
        action: hash
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 30s
    num_traces: 100000
    expected_new_traces_per_sec: 2000
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code:
          status_codes: [ERROR]
      - name: baseline
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic:
          sampling_percentage: 5
  batch: {}
exporters:
  otlp:
    endpoint: trace-store.example.com:4317
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, attributes, tail_sampling, batch]
      exporters: [otlp]
blocks.caption: Illustrative Collector Contrib tail tier: error OR probability selection, with no upstream head sampler. SDKs export all spans and the upstream gateway routes by trace id. Buffer settings are assumptions to load-test, not a retention guarantee; late spans, memory refusal or transport loss invalidate the complete-delivery estimate. Configure the backend endpoint and credentials for deployment.
